comment: Every place this package's ESLint config deliberately differs from the shared config in @mnaoumov/typescript-dev-toolkit, and why.
`scripts/eslint-config.ts` is a HAND COPY of that shared config rather than a call of its `defineEslintConfigs`,
and a hand copy drifts silently, which it did for eighteen months. update-npm-deps.ps1 compares the two configs on
every dependency sweep, against the toolkit version installed here, and fails on anything not recorded here.
The comparison is DIRECTIONAL: only 'the shared config refined something and this copy never took it' is a
finding. A rule this package enables that the shared config turns off is printed as information and never fails,
because this copy is then the stricter one and the shared config's reasons for its own relaxations are
measurements about the trees it serves.
A key is the finding's identity exactly as the check prints it: <role>|<rule>|<kind>[|<detail>]. The
correspondence runs BOTH ways - an entry describing a divergence that no longer exists fails the sweep too, which
is what stops this file going stale the way the comments at the call sites did. Add `task` when the entry is an
adoption intended for later rather than a settled decision; it is then re-reported on every run.
`roles` names the file of this package compared at each role. Only the `script` role is compared by default.

script|no-console|level.why: The build, lint, docs and version scripts are CLI entry points whose output IS their interface, so printing to stdout is what they are for. The shared config leaves the rule on because it is written for library and plugin source, which has no business printing.

script|no-restricted-syntax|option|optio.why: Same selector, same severity - the message names this package's own escape hatch (`castTo<T>()` from src/internal/castTo.ts), which a shared config cannot name.
Same selector, same severity - the wording says `in this project`, because here the mock classes really are the canonical types rather than one package's convention.

script|unicorn/class-reference-in-static.why: Every static factory here names its own class on purpose, and each mock class redeclares its factories rather than overriding an inherited one. Swapping the class name for `this` would make an inherited factory build the subclass while its signature still says the base, and `strictProxy(value, App)` passes the class as a runtime value, where `this` is a different object entirely.

script|unicorn/filename-case|option|opti.why: Source files are named after the API they mock, so the name is dictated by Obsidian and the DOM rather than by a casing convention - `Array.prototype.ts`, `App.ts`, `createEl.ts`. Allowing camel, kebab and pascal keeps the rule catching genuinely inconsistent names while preserving that 1:1 mapping.

script|unicorn/no-thenable|level.why: `Setting.then()` and `BaseComponent.then()` are Obsidian's own public API - the chainable callback hook every settings tab is written against. These mocks cannot drop a member of the surface they exist to reproduce.

script|unicorn/no-top-level-side-effects.why: Build, lint and version scripts are CLI entry points; the top-level call IS the program. Scoped to `scripts/**/*.ts`, beside the same block's `unicorn/no-process-exit` relaxation.

script|unicorn/prefer-dom-node-remove|le.why: Obsidian's `Component` has its own `removeChild(component)` for the component lifecycle, unrelated to `Node#removeChild`. The rule matches on the method name alone, so every report here is a component being unloaded, and following the advice calls a `remove()` that does not exist.

script|unicorn/prefer-global-this|level.why: These mocks reproduce the Obsidian renderer, where `window` and `document` are the canonical globals and the source being mirrored spells them that way - `Node.prototype.doc` falls back to the global `document` verbatim because Obsidian's own implementation does. Rewriting them to `globalThis` would make the mock stop reading like the API it stands in for.
